## AI in practice, not in theory {.welcome-slide}

::: {.welcome-intro}
This is a **hands-on bootcamp** about applying AI to real analytical work—with tools and workflows available in the World Bank environment.
:::

:::: {.welcome-grid}

::: {.welcome-card}
<h3>Bring your work</h3>
Try AI workflows on your own project, with guidance and technical support from instructors.
:::

::: {.welcome-card}
<h3>Build your pathway</h3>
Start with the foundations, then choose topics that fit your experience, interests, and work program.
:::

::: {.welcome-card}
<h3>Explore the research cycle</h3>
Work with practical examples spanning data and surveys, analysis, research outputs, and reproducibility.
:::

::: {.welcome-card}
<h3>Leave ready to apply</h3>
Build confidence with useful workflows you can adapt and reuse in your day-to-day work.
:::

::::

::: {.welcome-takeaway}
**Bring a real task—we'll help you find where AI makes it faster or better.**
:::

::: {.notes}
~1 minute 30 seconds. Open with: "Welcome. This is not another lecture on the potential of AI." Then set the practical tone. This bootcamp is not just about AI capabilities: it is about applying tools and workflows in the World Bank environment. Encourage participants to bring a real task or project. They will have opportunities to work on their own projects with instructor guidance and technical support. The program progresses from foundational to advanced sessions, so participants can shape a pathway around their experience, interests, and work programs. Sessions span different stages of analytical work, from data and surveys through research outputs and reproducibility.
:::

## Who we are {.team-slide}

Impact Analytics is part of the World Bank's Development Impact Group. Its mission is to strengthen the **transparency, credibility, and reproducibility** of research.

::: {.notes}
~1 minute 15 seconds. Impact Analytics brings concepts from data science and computer science into development research. Over the past decade, the team has developed open-source, open-access tools, processes, and trainings that support the full research production cycle, and partners with the World Bank Group Institute for Economic Development on e-learning that extends these methods globally. Briefly introduce the six instructors; they will sit at tables with participants and provide dedicated support throughout the course. Source: [Impact Analytics](https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/unit/unit-dec/impactevaluation/analytics).
:::

## BASELINE_TITLE {#who-you-are}

![](images/baseline-common-uses.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Baseline percentages of work-AI users who use AI for writing or editing documents, for background research, and who have used third-party chat AI."}

::: {.callout-note-custom}
You mostly use AI for writing and background research, through chat interfaces.
:::

::: {.notes}
~1 minute. These percentages come from the raw baseline responses (n = BASELINE_TOTAL). The bars are among the BASELINE_WORK_USERS work-AI users; any AI use (work or personal) is in the chart footnote. Writing and background research refer to the last four weeks; third-party chat AI is an ever-used tool question. Chat-tool use and background research are separate items, not a measured pairing. This is a cohort baseline, not an estimate for all WBG staff, and people who signed up for an AI bootcamp are likely heavier users than average.

Before advancing, ask for a show of hands: "Who has used a coding agent?" The next slide shows the baseline answer.
:::

## BASELINE_WORKFLOW_TITLE {#research-workflows}

![](images/baseline-research-workflows.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Baseline percentages of work-AI users who use AI for data analysis, surveys, dashboards or web apps, and reproducibility packages, plus the share who have ever tried a coding agent."}

::: {.callout-note-custom}
**Coding agents can change this**—they work with your files and code, not just chat. **BASELINE_CODING_PERCENT** have tried one; our goal: **everyone by the end of the Bootcamp**.
:::

::: {.notes}
~1 minute 30 seconds. Compare the show of hands with the coding-agent bar (BASELINE_CODING_PERCENT). The less-used workflows are data analysis/visualization, surveys, dashboards/web apps, and reproducibility packages; these refer to AI use in the last four weeks among BASELINE_WORK_USERS work-AI users, while the coding-agent bar is ever used. Coding agents are a practical way to expand how we use AI across research workflows because they work directly with files and code. 100% participation by endline is an aspiration, not an observed result.
:::

## What we'll do: apply AI workflows across the research cycle {.day-overview}

:::: {.welcome-grid}

::: {.welcome-card}
<h3>Day 1 · Agentic AI at the WBG</h3>
Understand agents; onboard them to a project; use prompts, memory files, and skills; work efficiently and safely.
[**Leave with:** a project memory file and a reusable skill, installed and used.]{.card-output}
:::

::: {.welcome-card}
<h3>Day 2 · Data acquisition and analysis</h3>
Apply AI to surveys, transcription, data quality, code improvement, and reproducible tables and charts.
[**Leave with:** an AI-programmed survey, data-quality checks, improved code, and a table or chart.]{.card-output}
:::

::: {.welcome-card}
<h3>Day 3 · Reproducible research products</h3>
Use AI for literature, presentations, working papers, reproducibility packages, and an adoption plan.
[**Leave with:** a presentation or policy brief, a reproducibility package, and an adoption plan.]{.card-output}
:::

::: {.welcome-card}
<h3>Day 4 · Advanced workflows (optional)</h3>
Explore advanced tools: dashboards, multi-agent workflows, geospatial analysis, and more.
[**Leave with:** hands-on practice with advanced AI tools and workflows.]{.card-output}
:::

::::

::: {.welcome-takeaway}
**Bring a real project.** Your outputs will reflect the sessions you attend.
:::

::: {.notes}
~1 minute 30 seconds. Give the arc, not a session-by-session tour: agent foundations, data work, research products, then advanced/scalable workflows. For each day, name the tangible output, not a promise of identical products for every participant. Day 1: a project memory file and a skill installed and used. Day 2: an AI-programmed survey, reusable data-quality checks, reviewed/improved code, and a table or chart; the survey and data checks can use demo materials. Day 3: a presentation or policy brief, reproducibility package, and adoption plan with 6-week and 3-month targets. Day 4 is optional and geared toward people ready for more advanced practice: a MEGA workspace and successful World Bank AI API query, AI outputs reviewed through GitHub, and a multi-agent workflow. Encourage participants to leave with workflows they can apply to their own projects.
:::

## How this works {.how-slide}

:::: {.welcome-grid}

::: {.welcome-card}
<h3>Learn by doing</h3>
More than half of the sessions are hands-on. Work on your own project, or practice with the demo materials.
:::

::: {.welcome-card}
<h3>Ask for help anytime</h3>
Instructors sit at your tables and provide dedicated support throughout. You can also post in the Teams channel.
:::

::: {.welcome-card}
<h3>Protect your data</h3>
Share data only with tools cleared for its classification. Today's session *How We Use AI Matters* covers the rules.
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
~1 minute. Set expectations for the format. Hands-on time is where most of the learning happens; participants without a suitable project can use the demo materials. Instructors sit at tables with participants and provide dedicated support throughout the course, and the Teams channel is the place for questions between sessions. Before anyone uploads project files to an AI tool, they should know the file's information classification and which tools are cleared for it; the Day 1 ethics session walks through the classification and tool-clearance rules in detail.
:::
